title: turn compression efficiency benchmark (proto)
content:
Context:
This is a proto write-up for the turn-compression experiments we ran between 2027-05-28 and 2027-06-07. The idea: apply a small summarization/compression step on long user turns to reduce token volume sent to the main model, thereby decreasing per-session token cost. We wanted to measure net effect on latency (extra step) vs token savings and end-to-end cost per active session.

Motivation / where this fits:
- E2E cost = cost(compression model) + cost(primary model)
- Goal: reduce cost(primary model) enough that it outweighs the extra compression cost while keeping p95/p99 latency impact acceptable for interactive flows (target p95 <= 400ms for tier-1).
- Use cases: chat-style assistants with long user messages (document ingestion, customer support transcripts).

High-level experiment matrix (configs tested):
1) baseline: no compression, direct to primary model (redwood-large-v1)
2) early compress (compress every user turn longer than 120 tokens using small model: rdl-mini-1)
3) on-evict compress (only compress when session token window > 8k or cache eviction imminent)
4) async compress (send turn to primary model immediately while background compression runs to update KV-cache later; optimistic primary cost + later correction)

Hardware / model choices:
- Primary: redwood-large-v1 @ H100 (quantized fp16), price reference: $0.045 / 1k tokens serving cost (internal estimate)
- Compression: rdl-mini-1 @ A10G (or CPU if < 64 tokens), price reference: $0.0025 / 1k tokens for cheap micro-model
- Traffic sample: 50k synthetic sessions from production trace (week of 2027-05-01), average request mix skewed toward long user turns (median user turn tokens = 180, 75th = 420)

Metrics captured (for each config):
- avg_tokens_sent_primary_per_session
- avg_tokens_sent_compression_per_session
- net_tokens (primary + compression)
- cost_per_session_usd (using internal token pricing)
- p50/p95/p99 latency end-to-end (ms)
- token-saved-% relative to baseline
- quality proxy: rouge-l/compression-bleu (very rough), and a small manual eval of 40 sessions for failure modes

Representative results (numbers are aggregated; this is an experiment snapshot):

ASCII table: aggregated per-session averages

config                | primary_tok | comp_tok | net_tok | cost_usd/session | p95_ms | p99_ms | tok_saved%
----------------------+-------------+----------+---------+------------------+--------+--------+---------
baseline              | 1250        | 0        | 1250    | 0.0563           | 310    | 760    | 0.0
early-compress       | 820         | 60       | 880     | 0.0402           | 370    | 840    | 29.6
on-evict-compress   | 980         | 35       | 1015    | 0.0466           | 330    | 780    | 18.8
async-compress       | 1200        | 60*     | 1260    | 0.0574           | 340    | 610    | -0.8

*async comp_tok counts background compression cost amortized when it ran; in some runs async reduced p99 due to optimistic first-pass but increased total tokens in a minority of sessions.

Interpretation: 
- Early-compress yields the largest token savings (~30%) and largest cost drop (~28.6% reduction vs baseline). But tail latency (p99) worsened by ~80ms and some runs show higher variance (we hit a p99 > 800ms occasionally).
- On-evict compress gives modest savings with smaller latency penalty; might be favorable for tight-SLO tiers.
- Async compress is attractive for p99: if compression happens after initial response it reduces observed tail in some cases but increases cost slightly overall because we often duplicate tokens in primary + compressed update. Only useful if KV-cache patching reduces downstream token growth substantially.

Quality and failure modes (notes from manual eval, 40 sessions):
- Compression occasionally loses critical named entities (6/40) when model aggressive; downstream LLM finished hallucinated details when user later referenced them — leads to degraded UX.
- Short-turn compression (<180 tokens) produced more harm than benefit because compression overhead and noise offset token savings.
- Async mode sometimes produced inconsistent assistant replies when the compressed summary omitted clarifying context the primary model used; visible when users referenced the same long-turn later.

Cost math sketch (how cost_usd/session derived):
- price_primary = $0.045 / 1k tokens -> baseline 1250 token -> 1.25 * 0.045 = 0.05625
- price_comp = $0.0025 / 1k tokens -> early compress avg 60 tokens -> 0.06 * 0.0025 = 0.00015
- net cost = primary_cost + comp_cost (simple)

Latency breakdown (approx, p95 slices):
- baseline: network (60ms) + model queuing (90ms) + decode (160ms) = 310ms
- with compression: extra compress step (80-120ms p95) + similar primary decode but with smaller decode time (proportional to tokens) -> net p95 up 50-70ms typical

Visual-ish sparklines (p95 latency by config):
- baseline     : ▂▄▆█▇▆▅▃ (p95=310)
- early-compress: ▂▄▅█▇█▆▅▄ (p95=370)
- on-evict     : ▂▄▆█▆▅▃▂ (p95=330)
- async        : ▂▄▆▅█▅▃▂▁ (p95=340)

Sensitivity notes (what changed results):
- Compression model size/quality: moving from rdl-mini-1 -> rdl-tiny reduced latency but produced worse quality and smaller token savings. The sweet spot in our tests was rdl-mini-1.
- Threshold tuning (we used 120 tokens): raising to 200 tokens reduces compression events by ~25% and lowers p99 impact while keeping ~70% of token savings.
- Hardware: running compression on CPU (cheap) starts to make sense only when compression model <= 32M params; otherwise A10G or small GPU yields better latency-cost tradeoff.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Can we make compression model deterministic and constrained to preserve named entities? (RNW-1823 / design doc linked)
- Better async reconciliation: can we patch KV-cache without duplicating tokens? Explore delta-only compression outputs.
- UX/monitoring: add a quality regression alert tied to compression-enabled rollout (sampled pairwise evals, expose "compression_applied" tag in traces).
- Cost accounting: attribute compress cost to feature flag / session cohorts so billing is clear for Dedicated customers.

Proposed rollout strategy (for product/console):
- Phase 0: small internal canary (5% of traffic, on-evict config). Monitor p99, quality signal.
- Phase 1: early-compress for long-turn-heavy product (customer-support bot) behind feature flag; require manual QA with 250 sampled sessions.
- Phase 2: gradual ramp to 50% if quality and p99 within thresholds, and add auto-threshold tuning for token-length cutoff.

Action items (owners):
- Maya: prepare canary config and metrics dashboard (RNW-2349) — due 2027-06-18
- Ravi: prototype deterministic entity-preservation constraint for rdl-mini-1 and run small eval (PR #418) — due 2027-06-25
- Jordan: update cost attribution in Console to tag compression costs per session cohort (Linear RNW-1976) — due 2027-07-02
- Sofia: manual evaluation batch and writeup (40->200 sessions) — due 2027-06-22

Notes to reviewers: this is intentionally rough. I want feedback on the suggested thresholds and whether async compression is worth the engineering complexity. Also input on metrics to add (suggestions: downstream token growth over a 10-turn window, cache-patch duplication rate).

References and related docs:
- TurnCompression-Design-V1 (confluence)
- Linear RNW-1823, RNW-1976, RNW-2349
- runtime PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/418

End.
